articles.title: When do linear equations have infinitely many solutions?
articles.learningObjective: Use elimination to distinguish a contradiction from a redundant equation, and verify that a variable remains free.
articles.example: Two purchases of the same fruit lead either to the same bill or an impossible conflicting bill.
articles.targetQuestionText: The equations x + 5y + 6z = 4, 2x + 3y + 4z = 7 and x + 6y + az = b have infinitely many solutions. Which relation holds: b − a = 3, a − b = 3, a + b = 11, or a + b = 12?

pyqs.independentSolution: R2−2R1 gives −7y−8z=−1. R3−R1 gives y+(a−6)z=b−4. Seven times second reduced row plus first gives (7a−50)z=7b−29. Infinite solutions require a=50/7,b=29/7. Then z=t,y=(1−8t)/7,x=(23−2t)/7 satisfies all equations. First two coefficient rows are independent, so exactly one free variable.

R3−4R2 gives (β−4α)z=−2. If coefficient nonzero, z is fixed, and x/y block determinant −3 gives a unique solution. If β=4α contradiction 0=−2 means no solution. The source omits α≠0; at α=β=0 the system has no solution but ratio undefined. Adaptation explicitly adds α≠0, disclosed in article.

articles.title: Why does mgh fail far above Earth?
articles.learningObjective: Use changes in −GMm/r and energy conservation when gravity varies with distance.
articles.example: Lift one small payload from the surface to a height twice Earth’s radius, then follow its fall in the reverse direction.

pyqs.independentSolution: Initial radius R; final radius 3R. ΔU=GMm(1/R−1/3R)=2GMm/(3R)=2mgR/3. Positive and below mg(2R). For h≪R the exact expression mgRh/(R+h) reduces to mgh; as h→∞ it approaches mgR.

Explicitly start from rest at infinity and neglect atmosphere/rotation. Initial total energy zero; K=GMm/R=mgR=1×9.8×6.4e6=6.272e7 J. v=√(2gR)=11199.999... m/s. Other celestial bodies and Earth recoil ignored.

articles.targetQuestionText: A mass m is moved from Earth’s surface to a height 2R above it. Earth’s radius is R and its surface gravitational acceleration is g. What is the increase in gravitational potential energy?

articles.title: How does concentration change a cell’s voltage?
articles.learningObjective: Derive n and Q from the balanced cell reaction, then use the sign of the Nernst correction to check concentration calculations.
articles.example: One zinc atom supplies the two electrons needed to turn two dissolved silver ions into silver metal.

pyqs.independentSolution: Zn+2Ag+→Zn2++2Ag, n=2, E°=0.80−(−0.76)=1.56 V. In the exam concentration approximation Q=1/x². E=1.56−0.059/2 log(1/x²)=1.56+0.059 log x. Thus log x=(1.60−1.56)/0.059=4/5.9, x≈4.764. Since E>E°, Q<1; consistent. Activities are dimensionless; concentration values stand for activities only under the question’s model.

Compare standard reduction potentials +0.07 V and −0.88 V. Keep AgBr reduction; reverse the iron half-reaction. Double AgBr coefficients to cancel two electrons, without doubling its potential. E°=0.07−(−0.88)=0.95 V. Iron is oxidised and potential is intensive; correct original option is the balanced overall reaction.

articles.targetQuestionText: At 298 K, a zinc–silver cell has [Zn²⁺] = 1 mol/L and a measured voltage of 1.60 V. The standard reduction potentials are −0.76 V for Zn²⁺/Zn and +0.80 V for Ag⁺/Ag. If x is the numerical value of [Ag⁺] in mol/L, find log₁₀ x. Use 2.303RT/F = 0.059 V.

articles.title: How do measurement errors combine in a formula?
articles.learningObjective: Estimate the first-order maximum fractional error in a product or quotient, including the multiplier from a power.
articles.example: A measured cylinder has density 4m/(πd²l); a larger measured diameter lowers the calculated density.

pyqs.independentSolution: ρ=4m/(πd²l); Δρ/ρ≈Δm/m+2Δd/d+Δl/l. Percentage contributions: 0.0205297, 0.1980198, 0.5988024. Total 0.8173519%=0.82%. All input errors zero gives zero output error; exact extrema bracket the first-order estimate. This is a maximum-error estimate, not independent-random-error quadrature.

R=V/I=2 Ω. Treat the stated least counts as input uncertainty estimates, as intended by the exam. ΔV=0.500 V, ΔI=0.200 A; ΔR/R≈0.5/10+0.2/5=0.09. ΔR≈0.18 Ω. Do not subtract the errors because the denominator can vary in the opposite direction. Exact Rmax=10.5/4.8=2.1875 Ω; first-order estimate is not an exact bound.

articles.title: How do you find partial pressures at equilibrium?
articles.learningObjective: Use the reaction mole balance to find equilibrium amounts, then distinguish partial pressures from total pressure.
articles.example: A sealed rigid flask contains inert helium while one mole of A partly changes into B.

pyqs.independentSolution: Write nA=1−x, nB=x, nHe=1. Kc=(x/10)/((1−x)/10)=x/(1−x)=4, so x=0.8 mol. RT/V=0.082×400/10=3.28 atm per mol. pHe=3.28, pB=2.624, pA=0.656; sum 6.56 atm and pB/pA=4. He absent from equilibrium expression but present in total pressure.

pyqs.answer: Kp = px²/(a²−x²), in the paper’s pressure convention
pyqs.independentSolution: Start with only a mol A in A⇌B+C; equilibrium amounts a−x,x,x and total a+x, not a. Partial pressures are p(a−x)/(a+x), px/(a+x), px/(a+x). Kp=pB pC/pA=px²/[(a+x)(a−x)]. Domain a>0,0<x<a. Dimensionless thermodynamic K uses p/p° instead of p; the article states the exam convention.

articles.title: How does new information change a probability?
articles.learningObjective: Combine disjoint weighted paths and restrict to the observed event to distinguish P(evidence|source) from P(source|evidence).
articles.example: A partly hidden city name shows AN; compare its five or seven possible adjacent-letter positions.

pyqs.independentSolution: The original omits the prior and reveal mechanism. Explicit adaptation: equal prior city probabilities; conditional on the city, select an adjacent pair uniformly. KANPUR has 5 pairs and one AN. ANANTPUR has 7 pairs and two AN. P(A|AN)=(1/2×2/7)/(1/2×1/5+1/2×2/7)=10/17, matching final key. Without these assumptions the answer is not uniquely determined. Cross-check 70 model letters from each city: 14 and 20 reveal AN, giving 20/34.

Captains A and B are exclusive and exhaustive with probabilities .6 and .4. Win routes have probabilities .6×.8=.48 and .4×.7=.28. Add to .76. Independent cross-check 100 model tournaments: 60 under A produce 48 wins; 40 under B produce 28. Bounds .7≤.76≤.8; unweighted average .75 is wrong.
